intro: Banks, hospitals, defence, government and critical-infrastructure customers often run software where nothing may reach the internet. In an air-gapped or tightly restricted environment there is no docker pull, no pip install, no hosted model API and no quick fix from your laptop. Every artefact must be carried in, verified and installed offline, and every upgrade repeated the same way. This lesson covers the spectrum from restricted VPCs to true air gaps, building a complete offline bundle, mirroring images and charts into the customer's registry, installing Kubernetes and your application offline, serving models without internet, and upgrading safely.
objectives: Distinguish connected, restricted, private-cloud and fully air-gapped environments
Build an offline bundle containing every image, chart, model and dependency
Mirror images and Helm charts into a customer registry and point workloads at it
Install Kubernetes and an application without internet access
Plan offline model serving, licensing, updates and support

rows: Outbound internet, maybe through a proxy
Firewall requests, mirrors for most dependencies
Private links to model and storage services, no public endpoints
No network path to the outside at all
Everything carried in on approved media and verified

blocks.text: Clarify early which one you face, and whether it differs between environments (development may be connected, production air-gapped). The answer reshapes the architecture: hosted model APIs become self-hosted models, telemetry becomes local, licence checks must work offline, and support moves from live access to support bundles carried out through the same approval process.

The core discipline is a **bill of materials** for the whole installation and a repeatable process that turns it into one verifiable bundle on a connected machine. Anything you forget will be discovered on the inside, where you cannot fetch it.

items: **Container images**: every image your charts reference, including init containers, sidecars and the images of any dependencies you install (databases, ingress, monitoring).
**Helm charts** at pinned versions, plus the values files.
**Kubernetes distribution** artefacts if you install the cluster too: binaries, its own images, install scripts.
**Model weights** and tokenizer files for self-hosted models, and the inference engine image.
**OS and language packages** if you install anything on hosts (often avoided by using images only).
**Checksums, signatures and SBOMs** for everything, and the documentation and installation script.

blocks.caption: On the connected side: export images and charts into a bundle
blocks.code:
mkdir -p bundle/images bundle/charts
while read -r img; do
  name=$(echo "$img" | tr '/:' '__')
  skopeo copy --all "docker://$img" "oci-archive:bundle/images/$name.tar:$img"
done < images.txt

helm pull oci://registry.yourproduct.example/charts/assistant --version 1.8.2 -d bundle/charts
(cd bundle && find . -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS -exec sha256sum {} \; > SHA256SUMS)
tar -czf assistant-1.8.2-offline.tar.gz bundle

blocks.text: Generate images.txt from the rendered chart (`helm template ... | grep 'image:'`) rather than by hand, and test the bundle by installing it into a cluster with outbound traffic blocked before it ever reaches the customer.

Inside the gap, the customer usually runs a registry (Harbor, Artifactory, Nexus, a cloud private registry). Push every image and chart into it after verifying checksums, then configure workloads and the cluster runtime to pull only from there.

blocks.caption: On the inside: verify, then push images and the chart to the internal registry
blocks.code:
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
for f in images/*.tar; do
  ref=$(skopeo inspect "oci-archive:$f" | jq -r '.Name')
  skopeo copy --all "oci-archive:$f" "docker://registry.corp.internal/mirror/${ref#*/}"
done
helm push charts/assistant-1.8.2.tgz oci://registry.corp.internal/charts

blocks.text: Point the chart at the mirror with `image.registry` and an `imagePullSecret`. For the cluster itself, container runtimes support **registry mirrors** so that references to public registries are transparently served from the internal one; with k3s this is the `registries.yaml` file, with other distributions the containerd mirror configuration. Mirroring public names avoids editing every manifest that references them.

sections.heading: Installing Kubernetes and the app offline

blocks.text: Often the customer provides the cluster. When you must install one, choose a distribution with a documented air-gap path. k3s, for example, ships an images archive that you place on each node and an install script that can skip downloading.

blocks.caption: k3s air-gapped server install (artefacts copied in beforehand)
blocks.code:
sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/images/
sudo cp k3s-airgap-images-amd64.tar.zst /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/images/
sudo install -m 0755 k3s /usr/local/bin/k3s
sudo mkdir -p /etc/rancher/k3s && sudo cp registries.yaml /etc/rancher/k3s/
INSTALL_K3S_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true ./install.sh
sudo k3s kubectl get nodes

blocks.text: Tools built for this problem package the whole thing. **Zarf**, an open-source air-gap package manager for Kubernetes, declares images, charts, manifests and files in a `zarf.yaml`, builds a single compressed package on the connected side (`zarf package create`), and on the inside initialises an in-cluster registry (`zarf init`) and deploys the package (`zarf package deploy`), rewriting image references automatically. Evaluate it before writing your own bundle scripts.

items: **Models**: hosted APIs are unavailable, so serve open-weight models inside with vLLM or a similar engine; carry weights in the bundle, size GPUs with the inference track's arithmetic, and set the engine to offline mode (for Hugging Face tooling, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`).
**Licences**: licence checks must work offline, typically with a signed licence file verified locally.
**Updates**: each release is a new bundle with release notes, checksums and a tested upgrade path; never patch inside by hand. Security updates for base images need a cadence the customer agrees to.
**Time and certificates**: internal NTP and an internal CA; certificate expiry inside a gap is a classic outage.

**Support**: you will not get live access. Ship a support-bundle command that collects logs, configuration (secrets redacted) and versions into an archive the customer can review and send out through their approved channel.

blocks.text: Do not plan to 'just connect it for the install'. Air-gap policies exist for regulatory and security reasons; an exception request can take months and may never be granted.

practice.title: Install into a simulated air gap
steps: Create a VM (or a kind cluster in a Docker network) with outbound internet blocked by firewall rules, plus a local registry container reachable only from inside.
On a connected machine, render your chart, extract the image list, and build an offline bundle with skopeo and helm pull, including checksums.
Transfer the bundle into the isolated environment, verify checksums, and push images and the chart into the internal registry.
Install the chart pointing image.registry at the mirror and confirm no pod tries to reach the internet (check events for pull errors).
Build version 1.8.3 as a new bundle and perform an offline upgrade with helm upgrade --atomic.
Optionally repeat the exercise with Zarf and compare the effort.

focus: Find out exactly how isolated each environment is, early.
A bill of materials and one verifiable bundle per release.
Mirror every image and chart into the customer registry; pull only from there.
Test the bundle in a blocked-network cluster before delivery.
Self-host models; offline licences; internal NTP and CA.
Support via redacted support bundles, not live access.

items.desc: Hugging Face tooling: never try to download
Set up in-cluster registry and tooling

pitfalls: Forgetting init-container, sidecar or dependency images in the bundle.
Assuming a temporary internet exception will be granted for the install.
Hosted model APIs or online licence checks in an air-gapped design.
Patching inside the gap by hand instead of shipping a new bundle.
No internal NTP or CA plan, then certificates expire silently.

quiz.q: Pods in the air-gapped cluster fail with ImagePullBackOff for a sidecar you never listed. What process fix prevents this?
options: Derive images from the rendered chart; test offline
Ask the customer to allow internet access for pulls
Use the latest tag so that images are always found
Build the missing images inside the air gap by hand
quiz.explain: Generating the list from rendered manifests catches every image, and a blocked-network test proves the bundle is complete before delivery.

quiz.q: Why mirror public registry names in the container runtime's mirror configuration?
options: Public image names resolve to the internal registry
It makes the container images noticeably smaller
It removes the need for checksums on the bundle
Mirrors bypass the customer's image security scanning
quiz.explain: Runtime mirror configuration redirects pulls for public names to the internal registry, so third-party manifests work without editing every image reference.

quiz.q: Your design uses a hosted LLM API. The production environment is air-gapped. What must change?
options: Serve an open-weight model inside the environment
Route requests through the customer's proxy
Cache API responses on a USB drive
Nothing, because APIs work through firewalls
quiz.explain: An air gap has no path to external services, so models must run inside on the customer's hardware.

quiz.q: What is the right way to apply a fix to an air-gapped deployment?
options: Ship a new checksummed bundle and upgrade normally
Edit the files directly inside the running containers
Ask for temporary remote access to patch it live
Email the changed source files to the operators
quiz.explain: Reproducible bundles keep every environment consistent and auditable; hand patches create drift nobody can reproduce.

quiz.q: How do you get diagnostic information out of an air-gapped customer site?
options: A redacted support bundle they review and send out
Live SSH access through your own personal VPN
Screenshots of the whole cluster dashboard, emailed
Telemetry sent to your own cloud automatically
quiz.explain: Customers control what leaves the gap; a redacted, reviewable support bundle respects that while giving you what you need.
